name: Argentina drought
text: Three La Niña years in a row left Argentina's farm belt parched. The WMO reported that September–December 2022 brought less than half the normal rainfall, the lowest in 35 years, and that farm exports were expected to fall 28% in 2023.

alt.t: WMO: drought in Argentina

name: Australia's 2019 drought and Black Summer
text: 2019 was Australia's warmest and driest year on record, with rainfall about 40% below average. The dried-out landscape fed the 2019–20 Black Summer bushfires, which burned around 24 million hectares.

alt.t: Bureau of Meteorology: Annual climate statement 2019

name: Queensland floods
text: One of the strongest La Niña events in a century gave Queensland its wettest December on record. Floods put 78% of the state under a disaster declaration, and about 20,000 homes in Brisbane were flooded in January 2011.

alt.t: Bureau of Meteorology: special climate statement

name: Amazon drought
text: A second year of drought pushed Amazon rivers to record lows. In October 2024 the Rio Negro at Manaus fell to its lowest level in 122 years of measurements, and fires burned around 46 million hectares across Brazil that year.

alt.t: EUSPA / Copernicus: record drought on the Rio Negro

name: Storm Daniel
text: Storm Daniel dropped 759 mm of rain on Zagora in a single day on 5 September 2023 and flooded the Thessaly plain, which produces about a sixth of Greece's farm output. 17 people died in Greece and damage passed €2 billion.

alt.t: NASA Earth Observatory: Greece's agricultural heartland underwater

name: Pakistan floods
text: Record monsoon rain flooded roughly a tenth of Pakistan in 2022, and Sindh got more than five times its usual rainfall. About 33 million people were affected, 1,739 died, and the World Bank put the damage at around US$40 billion.

alt.t: NASA Earth Observatory: Lake Manchar is overflowing

name: East Africa short-rains floods
text: One of the strongest positive Indian Ocean Dipole events since 1961 warmed the western Indian Ocean in late 2019. East Africa got about three times its normal rainfall, and floods hit Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia and Uganda.

alt.t: ICPAC: October–December 2019 extreme floods

name: Southern Africa drought
text: An El Niño-driven drought wrecked the 2023–24 growing season. Zambia declared a national disaster on 29 February 2024, and as hydropower failed, the utility ZESCO began daily power cuts of 8 hours, later 12.

alt.t: World Weather Attribution: El Niño key driver of drought

name: El Niño drought in southern Africa
text: The 2015–16 El Niño brought one of southern Africa's worst droughts. SADC declared a regional drought disaster in March 2016, and South Africa's maize crop was forecast 47% below its five-year average.

alt.t: USDA: South Africa El Niño drought

name: East Africa drought and Somalia famine
text: Failed rains in 2010 and 2011 caused East Africa's worst drought in about 60 years. The UN declared famine in parts of Somalia on 20 July 2011, and around 260,000 people died, half of them children under five.

alt.t: UN News: Somalia famine death toll

name: US drought
text: At its peak in July 2012, about 64% of the contiguous United States was in drought, an extent comparable to the 1930s and 1950s. Crop losses across the Midwest cost more than $35 billion.

alt.t: drought.gov: how the central US drought of 2012 evolved

name: UK summer floods
text: May to July 2007 was the wettest in England and Wales in records going back to 1766. The June and July floods killed 13 people and caused about £6.5 billion in damage.

alt.t: Met Office: record rainfall May–July 2007

name: The UK's sunniest spring
text: With 653 hours of sunshine, spring 2025 was the UK's sunniest since the series began in 1910, beating 2020 by more than 27 hours. It was also the warmest spring on record.

alt.t: Met Office: spring 2025 warmest and sunniest on record

name: The lockdown spring
text: Spring 2020 gave the Netherlands 805 hours of sunshine against a normal of 517, the most since 1901. Many people credited the COVID-19 lockdown, but KNMI found the weather pattern did it. Cleaner air made the sky bluer but added only a few percent of sunshine.

wiki.t: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the environment

alt.t: KNMI: sunny spring was not caused by the lockdown

name: The 2018 heatwave summer
text: Summer 2018 gave Denmark 802 hours of sunshine, the most since records began in 1920, and July 2018 was the sunniest month ever measured there. It tied 1997 as Denmark's warmest summer.

alt.t: DMI: summer 2018 overview (Danish)

name: The washout summer
text: After a spring that started in drought, April and June 2012 were each the wettest on record and the summer was the UK's wettest since 1912. Floods killed at least 9 people and caused about £1 billion in insured losses.

alt.t: Met Office: record rainfall April–July 2012

name: Storm Celia's Saharan dust
text: Storm Celia drew a huge plume of Saharan dust over Spain in mid-March 2022 and turned the skies yellow and orange. 107 of Spain's 471 air-quality stations recorded historically high PM10 levels.

alt.t: Copernicus CAMS: Saharan dust heads north

name: Arctic sea ice record low
text: On 16 September 2012 Arctic sea ice shrank to 3.41 million km², 18% below the previous record set in 2007 and 49% below the 1979–2000 average.

alt.t: NSIDC: Arctic sea ice extent settles at record seasonal minimum

name: Antarctic sea ice collapse
text: Antarctic sea ice stayed far below anything seen before through the 2023 winter. Its September maximum, 16.96 million km², was nearly 1 million km² below the previous record low from 1986.

alt.t: CIRES / NSIDC: Antarctic sea ice hits record low maximum

name: Antarctic sea ice record high
text: Antarctic sea ice grew slowly for decades and peaked at a record 20.11 million km² on 22 September 2014, nearly four standard deviations above the 1981–2010 mean. From 2016 it began to decline fast.

alt.t: NOAA Climate.gov: Antarctic winter sea ice sets new record
